title: Electrostatics
summary: Charge, charging, Coulomb's law, fields, potential and capacitors.
cards.0.p: Protons carry (+) charge and electrons carry (−) charge. An object with equal numbers of protons and electrons is neutral. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Charge is q = n·e, and its unit is the coulomb.
cards.0.key: Charge is quantized. e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, and n is an integer. So an object cannot have a charge of 1.5e.
cards.0.once.soru: A neutral object loses 3 electrons. What is its charge?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: An object that loses electrons is left with 3 extra protons.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: It would be (−) if it had gained electrons.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: The numbers of protons and electrons are no longer equal.
cards.1.p: Conductors have free electrons, so charge spreads over the whole object. In insulators charge stays where it is placed.
cards.1.key: The particles that move in a metal are electrons. Protons stay fixed in the nucleus.
cards.1.etk.soru: Is this material a conductor or an insulator?
cards.1.etk.ogeler.2.2: Ions in the salty fluids of the body carry charge.
cards.1.etk.ogeler.3.2: Graphite is not a metal, but it has free electrons.
cards.1.etk.ogeler.8.2: Dry wood does not carry charge. It becomes conductive when wet.
cards.1.once.soru: You rub a metal rod held in your hand on wool, but the rod does not get charged. Why?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The charge escapes through your body to the ground
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: Metal and the body are conductors. The charge that forms flows to the ground.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: A metal held by an insulating handle does get charged.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.yazi: Wool does not give up electrons
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: Electrons do transfer during rubbing. The problem is that the charge escapes.
cards.2.p: When two objects are rubbed together, electrons pass between them. The object that gives up electrons becomes (+) and the one that gains them becomes (−). The charges are equal in size and opposite in sign. A plastic rod rubbed on wool becomes (−).
cards.2.key: Usually two insulators are rubbed together, and which one gives up electrons depends on the materials. By conservation of charge, the total charge of an isolated system does not change.
cards.3.p: If a charged conductor touches another conductor, the total charge is shared and both end up with the same sign. The charge divides in proportion to the radii (q₁/q₂ = r₁/r₂).
cards.3.svg#12: conducting spheres joined by a wire
cards.3.key: Spheres in contact reach the same potential, and identical spheres share the charge equally. If the total charge is zero, both spheres end up neutral.
cards.4.p: When a charged rod comes near without touching, the electrons in a conductor shift. This is called polarization. If you ground the conductor, then remove first the connection and then the rod, the conductor is left with the sign opposite to the rod.
cards.4.svg#7: result: charge opposite in sign to the rod
cards.4.key: If you remove the rod before cutting the connection, the charge flows back from the ground and the conductor stays neutral. The rod loses no charge. The charge comes from the ground or goes to it.
cards.5.p: An electroscope is a device that shows charge. If a charged object touches the knob, charge spreads to the leaves. The leaves get the same sign, repel each other and spread apart.
cards.5.key: When an object with the same sign comes near a charged electroscope, the leaves open wider. With the opposite sign they start to close. Open leaves alone do not show the sign.
cards.6.h: Charge on the outer surface and at sharp points
cards.6.p: On a charged conductor the excess charge spreads over the outer surface, and the field inside is zero. Charge concentrates at sharp points. A lightning rod uses this to carry lightning to the ground.
cards.6.svg#1: charge is on the outer surface,
cards.6.key: Charge can leak into the air from a sharp point. In a storm the inside of a metal-bodied car is safe, because the charge flows away over the outer surface.
cards.6.once.soru: Where does the excess charge on a charged metal sphere collect?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: The charges repel each other and move to where they can be farthest apart, the surface.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Like charges repel each other. So they cannot collect at the center.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: In a conductor charges move freely and are pushed to the surface. The inside of the conductor stays uncharged.
cards.7.p: The force between two point charges is F = k·q₁·q₂ / r², and k is about 9×10⁹ N·m²/C². The two charges exert forces on each other that are equal in size and opposite in direction.
cards.7.svg#7: equal size, opposite direction (even if q₁ ≠ q₂)
cards.7.key: The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance. If the distance doubles, the force drops to one quarter.
cards.7.etk.soru: Change the charges and the distance. F > 0 means repulsion and F < 0 attraction. What happens when the distance doubles?
cards.7.etk.yorum.1.1: One of the charges is zero, so there is no force.
cards.8.p: A charge creates an electric field around it. The field is E = F / q (N/C), and it is a vector. For a point charge E = k·q / r². Where the field lines are close together, the field is strong.
cards.8.key: A (+) charge feels a force along the field, and a (−) charge feels a force opposite to the field.
cards.9.p: Potential is the potential energy per unit charge. It is V = k·q / r, its unit is the volt, and it is a scalar. The difference between two points is called the voltage, and the work is W = q·ΔV.
cards.9.key: A volt equals a J/C. V has no direction, and you write it with the sign of the charge and add.
cards.9.once.soru: How many J of work does it take to move a 2 C charge through a voltage of 6 V?
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: You multiply charge and voltage. You do not divide them.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: You multiply charge and voltage. You do not add them.
cards.10.h: Field and potential of two charges
cards.10.p: Fields add as vectors, and potentials add as scalars. Midway between +q and −q the fields add up, but the potentials cancel, so V = 0.
cards.10.svg#0: Field is a vector, potential a scalar
cards.10.svg#7: At the midpoint: E = E₁ + E₂, toward −q
cards.10.key: Midway between two equal +q charges E = 0, but V ≠ 0. Where E is zero, V does not have to be zero.
cards.10.once.soru: What is the electric field exactly midway between two equal +q charges?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The two fields are equal in size and opposite in direction. So they cancel.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: Fields are vectors. Fields in opposite directions subtract. They do not add.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.yazi: Equal to that of one charge
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: The field of the second charge exactly cancels the first.
cards.11.p: Between oppositely charged parallel plates the field is uniform, and E = V / d. A charge feels a force F = q·E. A charge that crosses a voltage V gains an energy KE = q·V.
cards.11.key: The field is the same everywhere and points from the (+) plate to the (−) plate. The acceleration is a = q·E / m. An electron gains 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J (1 eV) across a voltage of 1 V.
cards.11.once.soru: The voltage between the plates is 100 V and the distance is 0.02 m. What is the field in V/m?
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: You divide the voltage by the distance. You do not multiply.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Voltage is not the field. To find the field, divide the voltage by the distance.
cards.12.p: A capacitor is two conducting plates with an insulator between them. It stores energy by storing charge. Capacitance is C = Q / V, and its unit is the farad. For a parallel-plate capacitor C = ε·A / d.
cards.12.key: ε is the permittivity of the insulator between the plates, and the stored energy is ½·Q·V. C depends only on how the capacitor is built. Changing Q or V does not change C.
cards.12.once.soru: If you move the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor closer together, what happens to its capacitance?
cards.12.once.secenekler.0.neden: C = ε·A / d, so when d gets smaller, C gets larger.
cards.12.once.secenekler.1.neden: As the plates get closer, the capacitance grows.
cards.12.once.secenekler.2.neden: Capacitance depends on the area of the plates and the gap between them.
cards.13.h: Capacitors in series and in parallel
cards.13.p: Capacitors in parallel have the same voltage, and their charges add (Ceq = C₁ + C₂). Capacitors in series have the same charge, and their voltages add (1/Ceq = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂).
cards.13.svg#12: C gets smaller in series and larger in parallel.
cards.13.key: In series the equivalent capacitance is smaller than the smallest capacitance. Two identical capacitors C give C/2 in series and 2C in parallel.
cards.13.once.soru: Two identical 4 μF capacitors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent capacitance in μF?
cards.13.once.secenekler.0.neden: In parallel the capacitances add, and 4 + 4 = 8 μF.
cards.13.once.secenekler.1.neden: 2 μF is what you get in series.
cards.14.p: The field inside a conductor is zero. A metal cage also shields its inside from outside fields, and it is called a Faraday cage. That is why the people inside a car struck by lightning are safe.
cards.14.svg#14: a metal cage keeps the outside field out
cards.14.key: The metal door of a microwave oven works the same way. A mesh with holes smaller than the wavelength does not let the wave through.
cards.14.once.soru: Which best explains why your phone often has no signal in an elevator?
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.yazi: The metal cabin blocks the waves
cards.14.once.secenekler.0.neden: Like a Faraday cage, the metal cabin keeps outside waves from getting in.
cards.14.once.secenekler.1.neden: What matters is the metal cabin, not the height.
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.yazi: There is little air in the cabin
cards.14.once.secenekler.2.neden: Radio waves do not need air to travel.
cards.15.p:
• Charge is quantized and conserved. In solids only electrons are transferred.
• Friction gives opposite signs, contact the same sign, and induction with grounding the opposite sign.
• On a conductor charge collects on the outer surface and at sharp points.
• The Coulomb force falls off as 1/r². E is a vector and V is a scalar.
• Capacitance is C = Q/V = ε·A/d.
quiz.0.q: Two point charges of 2 μC and 5 μC are 0.3 m apart. What is the electric force between them in N? (k = 9×10<sup>9</sup> N·m²/C², 1 μC = 10<sup>−6</sup> C)
quiz.1.q: What sign of charge does each object have? Put each one in the right group.
quiz.1.ogeler.1.0: An object that gives up electrons
quiz.1.e: An object that loses electrons, or has more protons than electrons, is (+). Glass rubbed on silk gives up electrons and becomes (+). The silk gains those electrons and becomes (−). A plastic rod rubbed on wool also becomes (−).
quiz.2.q: A voltage of 100 V is applied to parallel plates 2 cm apart. What is the electric force, in N, on a 2 μC charge between the plates?
quiz.2.e: E = V / d = 100 / 0.02 = 5000 V/m. Then F = q·E = 2×10<sup>−6</sup>·5000 = 0.01 N, and this force is the same everywhere between the plates.
quiz.3.q: Two identical 6 μF capacitors are connected in series, and 12 V is applied across them. Which statement is true?
quiz.3.o.0: The equivalent capacitance is 12 μF, and each capacitor has 12 V.
quiz.3.o.1: The equivalent capacitance is 3 μF, and each capacitor has 12 V.
quiz.3.o.2: The equivalent capacitance is 3 μF, and each capacitor has 6 V.
quiz.3.o.3: The equivalent capacitance is 6 μF, and each capacitor has 6 V.
quiz.3.e: In series 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6, so C = 3 μF. The charges and capacitances are equal, so the 12 V divides into 6 volts on each capacitor.
quiz.3.y.0: In series the capacitances do not add. You add their reciprocals: 1/C = 1/6 + 1/6.
quiz.3.y.1: Identical capacitors in series share the total voltage. Each one has 12/2 = 6 V.
quiz.3.y.3: In series the equivalent capacitance is smaller than a single capacitor: 6·6/(6+6) = 3 μF.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Rub the glass, touch the spheres together, charge by grounding and set the Coulomb force.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Charge does not appear from nothing. Only electrons pass from one object to the other. Rub the glass rod with the silk cloth.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: What charge does the glass rod have after rubbing?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The one that is (−) is the silk, which gains the electrons.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The glass gives electrons to the silk. The glass, now short of electrons, becomes (+), and the silk becomes (−) by the same amount. Total charge is conserved.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Two electrons moved to the silk. The glass is no longer neutral.
A:adimlar.1.metin: Spheres that touch share charge in proportion to their radii. Sphere A has 12 μC and B is neutral. Choose the radius of B so that B ends up with 8 μC after they touch.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: When the radii are 1 : 2, the 12 μC divides as 4 : 8. The total charge is still 12 μC. In contact, charge is conserved and both spheres get the same sign.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.ipucu: B must take 2/3 of the total.
A:adimlar.2.metin: A (−) charged rod approaches a neutral conducting sphere without touching it. The electrons in the sphere can move freely.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What happens to the side of the sphere near the rod?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Electrons are repelled by the (−) rod and escape to the far side.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The total charge is zero, but the charges shift.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Electrons are repelled and move to the far side. The near side becomes (+) and the far side (−). The sphere as a whole is still neutral. This is called polarization.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Now the order is: bring the rod near, connect the sphere to the ground, cut the connection, and remove the rod. Watch this sequence.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.soru: What charge is the sphere left with?
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The repelled electrons escape to the ground, and they cannot come back because the connection is cut first. The sphere is left with the sign opposite to the rod.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: An object charged by induction takes the sign opposite to the rod. Electrons left the sphere.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Charge can move without contact too. Here the electrons flowed to the ground.
A:adimlar.4.metin: A (+) rod has been brought near the knob of an electroscope. By induction the leaves get the same sign and repel each other. Move the rod away.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: What happens to the leaves when the rod moves away?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The induction weakens, and the charge on the leaves decreases.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: No charge passed to the electroscope. When the induction ends, the leaves go back to how they were.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: There was no contact, so the total charge of the electroscope is zero. When the rod moves away, the charges return to their places and the leaves close.
A:adimlar.5.metin: The force between two charges is F = k·q₁·q₂ / r². q₁ = +4 μC. Set q₂ and the distance so that the force is an attraction of 0.1 N (k ≈ 9·10⁹ N·m²/C²).
A:adimlar.5.gorev.tamam: For q₂ = −1 μC and r = 60 cm, F = 9·10⁹ · 4·10⁻⁶ · 1·10⁻⁶ / 0.36 = 0.1 N. Opposite charges attract, and like charges repel.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.ipucu: For attraction q₂ must be (−). At 30 cm, −1 μC gives 0.4 N. Double the distance.
A:adimlar.6.metin: Electric field lines show the direction a (+) test charge placed there would be pushed. Change the sign of the charge on the right.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.soru: Where do field lines start and where do they end?
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The lines point out of a (+) charge and into a (−) charge, and they never cross.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The direction of the field is the direction a (+) test charge would be pushed. That direction points away from a (+) charge.
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.yazi: They exist only between the two charges
A:adimlar.6.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The lines spread in every direction. For two charges of the same sign, an empty region is left between them.
A:kapanis.0: Charge is quantized (e = 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C) and conserved. In charging, only electrons are transferred.
A:kapanis.1: With friction, glass becomes (+) and silk (−). With contact, charge is shared in proportion to the radii and with the same sign.
A:kapanis.2: An object charged by induction and grounding gets the sign opposite to the rod. For this, the connection must be cut before the rod is removed.
A:kapanis.3: By Coulomb's law F = k·q₁·q₂ / r². Opposite charges attract and like charges repel.
A:kapanis.4: Field lines leave (+), enter (−), and never cross.
